name: E-commerce fulfillment
one_line: Stores, packs and ships online orders for merchants, so a brand doesn't have to run its own warehouse.
sells: Warehousing, pick-pack-ship, shipping and returns handling for online orders, charged per order plus storage
customers: Online merchants and brands, from solo sellers to large retailers, selling on their own sites and on marketplaces
suppliers: Warehouse space and labor, parcel carriers, warehouse robotics and software, and the platforms and marketplaces that route the orders

revenue.note: Analyst estimate; covers receiving, storage, pick-pack-ship, delivery and returns for online orders. Projected to grow ~12%/yr to ~$268B by 2031; North America is ~32% of it. Amazon's captive FBA network is the largest single operator but is not separately sized here.

structure.type: Dominant firm over a fragmented tail
structure.why: Amazon's in-house network (FBA) fulfills the bulk of U.S. marketplace orders and dwarfs every independent. Below it the outsourced-3PL market is structurally fragmented, mixing global contract-logistics giants (DHL, GXO) with venture-backed e-commerce-native 3PLs (ShipBob, ShipMonk, Stord), none with a dominant share.
structure.hhi_note: No published shares on a comparable basis. Mordor rates market concentration 'low' / structurally fragmented, but that view excludes Amazon's captive FBA volume, which would raise concentration sharply if counted.

econ: Economies of density: fulfillment gets cheaper and faster the more orders flow through a given warehouse and delivery zone, so the largest network delivers at the lowest cost per package and smaller merchants outsource rather than build their own. It is a make-vs-buy decision at heart, a merchant renting a shared fulfillment network the way it rents cloud servers, trading a per-order fee for scale it could never reach alone.
rank_basis: approximate e-commerce fulfillment scale (disclosed fulfillment revenue, GMV, order volume or network size); shares are not published on a comparable basis and the market is fragmented below Amazon

companies.name: Amazon (FBA & Multi-Channel Fulfillment)
companies.note: The dominant operator by far. Its captive FBA network fulfills most of the ~1.65M active third-party sellers' orders and also ships non-Amazon orders via Multi-Channel Fulfillment. Fulfillment revenue is bundled inside Amazon's third-party seller services (~$184B in 2025, which also includes commissions and ads).

companies.name: DHL Supply Chain
companies.note: World's largest contract-logistics operator (part of DHL Group); e-commerce fulfillment is one line of a broad warehousing business, so its revenue isn't separately disclosed.

companies.name: GXO Logistics
companies.note: Largest pure-play contract-logistics company (public); runs outsourced warehouses and returns for major retailers and brands, with e-commerce a big share of volume.

companies.name: ShipBob
companies.note: Leading e-commerce-native 3PL for SMB and mid-market merchants: 60+ fulfillment centers, 7,000+ merchants, 200M+ orders shipped. Asset-light (mostly partner warehouses); charges a per-shipment fee. 2023 revenue per Sacra.

companies.name: Flexport (Deliverr / Shopify Logistics)
companies.note: Took over Shopify's logistics arm, including Deliverr (which Shopify bought for $2.1B in 2022), in 2023; powers Shopify's merchant fulfillment. Announced a shift to an asset-light model by 2027.

companies.name: ShipMonk
companies.note: Venture-backed e-commerce 3PL (12 fulfillment centers across US, Canada, Mexico and EU; ~$365M raised); bundles fulfillment with order- and inventory-management software.

companies.name: Stord
companies.note: Cloud-supply-chain 3PL: 11 owned facilities plus a 1,000+ partner-warehouse network; ~$525M raised, crossed $200M ARR in 2022.

products_note: Flagship products and services as of Nov 2026, checked against each operator's site and recent coverage; most 3PLs here are private, so revenue and shares are disclosed only where a company has published them.
